explanations.answer: Send him on his way back home
explanations.explanation: Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), goes to Laban and says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” He's asking to go home, not to set up shop where he is. The request is about leaving, and Laban is the one who has to answer it.

explanations.answer: Give him a field of his own
explanations.explanation: Jacob never asks for a field here. What he asks is, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” Laban is Jacob's father-in-law, and he's the one hearing this request. Jacob has his eyes on home, not on a piece of land next door.

explanations.answer: Let him build a house nearby
explanations.explanation: Staying close by isn't what Jacob asks. He says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” A house next door would be a very short trip for a man talking about going home. The request points toward leaving.

I can see why you'd think it, but Jacob says the opposite. He tells Laban, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He's asking for his wives and children, so they're part of the request. Leaving them behind would be a strange way to ask for them.

Right, his family is part of the request. Jacob says, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He wants his wives and children given to him, not left with Laban. This family is not getting left at the rest stop, friend.

Laban says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Divination is a way of seeking hidden answers, and Laban says that's how he learned it. Whatever his method, he names the LORD's blessing and ties it straight to Jacob. That's Laban admitting Jacob is good for business.

No warning in sight, friend. Laban says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” That's the opposite of bad news. He's telling Jacob the blessing came with Jacob's name on it. And right after, he says, “Name your wages…” That's not how anybody talks when they've just been warned.

A test isn't what Laban says. He asks Jacob to stay first: “If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay.” Then he gives his reason: “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” I think Laban just did the math and didn't like the answer he got when he pictured Jacob leaving.

Jacob says it plain: “…you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over.” That's Jacob making his case to Laban. He doesn't leave it at that, though, because he goes on to ask when he can provide for his own household. I'd call that a strong opening argument.

Jacob really does say this to Laban. His words are, “…you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over.” He's pointing to how much Laban's flocks have grown under his care. Then he asks when he can provide for his own household.

Jacob asks for “…every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat.” Then he says, “These will be my wages.” He's naming animals by their markings and color. That's his whole offer, and it comes with one condition.
That one's flipped around. Jacob asks for the speckled or spotted sheep, the dark-colored lambs, and the spotted or speckled goats. Those are his wages. The plain ones stay with Laban.

Jacob doesn't ask for a fraction at all. He names kinds of animals: every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. He's picking by color, not by percentage. No calculator needed for this deal.

Jacob says, “…my honesty will testify for me when you come to check on my wages in the future.” He's inviting Laban to come look for himself. Then he spells out what would count against him: goats that are not speckled or spotted, or lambs that are not dark-colored, “…will be considered stolen.” That's a man leaving the cookie jar open and saying, “Count 'em.”

Jacob doesn't bring up patience here. He says “…my honesty will testify for me…” when Laban comes to check his wages. The flocks will tell the story. Patience may come in handy, but honesty is the word he used.

Kindness is a lovely word, but Jacob reaches for a different one. He says, “…my honesty will testify for me…” and then draws the line: any goats that are not speckled or spotted, or lambs that are not dark-colored, “…will be considered stolen.” That's a man handing his boss a ruler and saying, “Measure me.” I've had friends who wouldn't do that with a single cookie crumb.
Laban doesn't turn him down. He says, “Agreed.” Then he adds, “Let it be as you have said.” That's a yes with a bow on it, and Jacob has the deal.
Right, Laban takes the deal. He says, “Agreed,” and then, “Let it be as you have said.” No haggling, no counteroffer. I think that's a man who just wants to shake hands and move on.

Laban takes out the streaked or spotted male goats, the speckled or spotted female goats and every dark-colored lamb, and places them “…under the care of his sons.” Those are Laban's own sons. Notice it all happens “That very day…” and he doesn't wait around. I think a man that quick knows exactly what he's doing.

Jacob's sons are a good guess, but the text says Laban put the animals “…under the care of his sons.” That's Laban's own household. Then he puts a three-day journey between himself and Jacob (Genesis 30:36). Three days! I've had a longer trip to find the one good spatula in my kitchen. I think those animals just got a very quiet new neighborhood.

Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives (Genesis 29:23, 28), but they aren't who Laban picks. The text says he put the animals under the care of his sons. So the animals go to Laban's sons. Leah and Rachel aren't part of this handoff.

Jacob takes fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and peels the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So what shows is white wood. A peeled branch looks very different from a bark-covered one, and that's what he sets out.

Green sap makes sense if you're picturing a fresh branch, and these are fresh ones. But the text says Jacob peeled the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” White, friend, like a pale stripe on a dark stick. He lined those up at the watering troughs where the flocks would see them.

Dark wood is a fair guess, but the color is the other way around. The text says Jacob peeled the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So the branches had pale stripes where the bark came off. Then he set them in the watering troughs in front of the flocks.

Jacob sets the peeled branches “…in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The branches go right where the flocks come to drink. I think Jacob picked that spot with care. Location, location, location.

The pens aren't where Jacob puts the branches. He sets them in the watering troughs, in front of the flocks coming in to drink. That's where the animals come for water. Pens are for sleeping, and troughs are where the traffic is.

Not the open fields. The verse says Jacob set the peeled branches “…in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The branches go where the flocks come to drink. Jacob wasn't leaving them lying around the pasture.

The text says the flocks mated in front of the branches and “…bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” That's what came out of it. Genesis tells us what happened and doesn't explain why. I think Jacob was watching those lambs and kids closely.

They came out marked. The flocks “…bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” Plain ones aren't what the verse reports. Genesis just tells us what happened, and I bet Jacob took a good long look.
Jacob does the opposite. The text says he “…set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals.” His animals have their own space. No mixing allowed.

That's right, it's False, and Jacob is careful about it. The text says he “…set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals.” Two flocks, two sets of animals, and he keeps a clear line between them. Honestly, I've never kept my sprinkles and my chocolate chips that organized.

The verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” He only puts them out for the stronger females. The weaker ones don't get the branches. I think that's a man who knows exactly what he's doing.

Thirsty is a good guess, since these branches sit in the watering troughs. But the verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Strength is what Jacob checks, not thirst. The text says the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob (Genesis 30:42).

Young isn't the word. The verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Strength is what the text goes by here. Age doesn't come up, and a strong animal gets the branches while a weak one doesn't.
It goes the other way around. The text says “…the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob.” The stronger animals end up on Jacob's side of the ledger. Laban gets the weaker ones.

Right, the weaker ones go to Laban. The text says, “…the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob.” So Jacob ends up with the stronger animals. I think Laban got the short end of that stick.

The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a long way from asking when he could provide for his own household. I think his accountant would've been smiling.

explanations.answer: He loses most of his flocks
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way. It says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He ends up with large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. Nothing about losing his flocks.

Debt isn't in the picture. The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a long list of things, and a tab owed to Laban isn't on it.
